source: Nathen Harvey, 'Engineering leaders can't prove AI is paying off', LeadDev, published 26 November 2026 (article:published_time 2026-11-26T07:52:11Z). Dek: 'What 165 engineering leaders told us at LeadDev Berlin 2026.' Opened in full: https://leaddev.com/leadership/engineering-leaders-cant-prove-ai-is-paying-off
data_type: Survey (voluntary, anonymous, self-report) of conference attendees, plus free-text respondent quotes.
sample_and_method: From the article's 'About the survey' note: '165 LeadDev Berlin attendees (November 9–10, 2026) took a voluntary, anonymous survey. Results describe this group, not the wider industry, and show association, not causation.' Body text: 'Most were engineering managers and directors.' Usage groups: heavy = 'a lot' or 'a great deal' (64%), moderate = 'a moderate amount' (30%), light = 'a little' or 'not at all' (7%); 'As the light group is small (11), comparisons are mainly heavy versus moderate.' Recruitment: conference attendees at the event; no further sampling method, response rate or exact role counts are given. Figure 3 says workload and trust differences are 'statistically confirmed' but no test or numbers are given in text.
vendor_interest: Indirect. LeadDev is a media and events company (sells conference tickets and sponsorship), not an AI tool vendor. The author bio says Nathen Harvey 'is a Principal Technologist on the Developer Experience team at AWS', and AWS sells AI developer tooling. The article promotes no product.
headline_figures: 'That's what we heard from 165 LeadDev Berlin 2026 attendees in November. Most were engineering managers and directors. Nearly two-thirds (64%) say their team relies on AI "a lot" or "a great deal." Only 7% use it a little or not at all.'

'When we asked how teams measure the impact of AI, the most common answers described activity: delivery speed (52%) and adoption (45%). Business outcomes, such as revenue or customer satisfaction, came last at 20%.'
'When we asked what they find most rewarding about engineering work, helping their team succeed (34%) and delivering for customers (33%) far outranked pay or career growth (under 3% each).'
'Of the respondents who gave a view, 45% have little or no confidence that their team's measures are what senior leaders want. Only 20% are very or extremely confident.'
'One in four individual contributors don't know what their leaders want from AI. Not one director said the same.'
'Directors aren't immune: 40% have little or no confidence their own measures are what senior leaders want. However, not one said "I don't know."'

'Questions about whether AI is paying off rise with seniority, from 10% of individual contributors to 32% of directors. About one in five individual contributors and managers raised concerns about quality and risk. No director did.'
'Heavy AI users are far more likely to report heavier workloads and to trust AI output but not reliably to feel more productive.'

'About two-thirds of teams have officially committed to at least one change for 2027, most often to how they deliver software. Many are also "letting practices emerge through experimentation" (57%). Structural changes are rarer: only 16% plan new roles.'

'Half of heavy AI users have committed to two or more changes, compared with a quarter of moderate users. Moderate users were nearly three times as likely to be experimenting with no concrete commitment at all (31% vs. 11%). The samples are small here so you should treat these gaps as directional.'
'Only 53% of individual contributors say their team has committed to a change, compared with 73% of engineering managers.'
metric_layer: Reports which layers teams measure: activity/delivery (delivery speed 52%) and input/usage (adoption 45%) dominate; financial/business outcome (revenue, customer satisfaction) is last at 20%. The survey itself measures self-reported perceptions (confidence in measures, workload, trust, felt productivity), not delivery or financial data. 'ROI came up more than anything else' when asked what leaders want.
respondent_role_split: Given for several items, as text (chart values for Figure 2 not transcribed): about one in four ICs don't know what leaders want vs no directors; 40% of directors have little or no confidence their measures match what senior leaders want, but none said 'I don't know'; questions about whether AI is paying off rise from 10% of ICs to 32% of directors; about one in five ICs and managers raised quality and risk concerns, no directors did; 53% of ICs vs 73% of engineering managers say their team has committed to a change. No executive tier is reported; per-role sample sizes are not given.
workload_signal: Strong. Heavy users are 'far more likely to report heavier workloads' (statistically confirmed per Figure 3) 'but not reliably to feel more productive' (productivity gap not statistically confirmed). 'Put simply: we can say with confidence that heavy users are working more. We can't say with confidence that they feel more productive.' Direction of causation unknown: 'Busy teams may reach for AI to cope, or AI may make it easier to take on more.' Author's hunch: load moves 'especially in review and verification'. Burnout quote from an engineering manager. Recommendation: 'Treat workload as a success measure. Check in on load explicitly, and make deciding what not to build part of planning.' No hours or time-correcting-AI figures.
definition_of_value_offered: Yes, as advice rather than a single definition. 'Name two or three business outcomes AI should move, such as faster time to customer value, fewer incidents, or lower cost per feature. Write them down and share them with the whole team, not just your peers.' 'Pair every activity metric with an outcome. Keep tracking AI-assisted pull requests, but put them next to your change failure rate. Keep reporting time saved, but check whether lead time to customer value actually drops. Attribution will be imperfect, so look for a consistent direction across several measures.' Also treat workload as a success measure and 'Put a date on your experiments. Pick a point in 2027 to review what you've learned, adopt what worked, stop what didn't'. Team questions include 'Would our current measures tell us if AI stopped helping?' and 'where did the time AI saved your team actually go?'
removal_counterfactual: No evidence. The article frames the question through a director's quote ('Would anyone notice if we stopped using AI tools?') and asks 'Would our current measures tell us if AI stopped helping?', but reports no data on teams without the tools. The light-use group (n=11) was too small for comparison. It says: 'None of this calls for slowing down. It calls for being more deliberate.'
key_quotes: "Would anyone notice if we stopped using AI tools?" (a director of engineering and heavy AI user, quoted in the article)
"We talk about efficiency but there is no [consensus] about what that is." (an engineering manager and heavy AI user, quoted in the article)
caveats: Self-report from a convenience sample of 165 conference attendees, mostly managers and directors; the article itself says results describe this group, not the industry, and show association, not causation. Per-role subgroup sizes are not given, so role splits (e.g. 'not one director') may rest on small counts. The 45%/20% confidence figures are among respondents 'who gave a view', a denominator not stated. Commitment comparisons between heavy and moderate users are flagged by the author as directional only. The usage split (64/30/7) sums to 101% from rounding. The productivity difference by usage is explicitly not statistically confirmed. Author works at AWS. This is the only write-up; no conflicting figures found.
access: Primary opened in full (raw HTML of the LeadDev page, full body text read). Not verified: exact values plotted in Figures 1-3 (images; only figures stated in text are used), the statistical method behind 'statistically confirmed', per-role counts, and the survey instrument. No separate survey report or dataset was linked.
